questions.question: Explain the role of the conidia in the life cycle of Fusarium, including their formation, dispersal, and germination.
questions.solution_html:
• and germination.
  • ▪ The members of the genus Fusarium typically produce two types of conidia that are termed
  • macroconidia and microconidia based on the size.
  • ▪ Macroconidia are long, multiseptate, crescent or fusiform in shape, and are generally borne in
  • sporodochia but may also occur separately.
  • ▪ Microconidia are very small conidia produced from the tips of simple or branched
  • conidiophores, which are indistinguishable from hyphae
  • ▪ The role of the conidia in the life cycle of Fusarium is dispersal. Conidia are non- motile and
  • are dispersed by wind, rain splash, irrigation water, insects, and farm tools.
  • ▪ Germination of Conidia
  • ▪ Under favourable conditions (moisture, warmth, and nutrient availability), conidia germinate
  • by producing germ tubes.

questions.question: Differentiate between upper cortex and lower cortex of Parmelia thallus.
questions.solution_html:
• Upper Cortex
  • ▪ Made of tightly packed fungal hyphae, forming a dense, thick-walled protective skin. May contain
  • specialized pores for gas exchange called pseudocyphellae, as well as vegetative reproductive
  • structures like isidia and soredia. It shields the internal algal layer from dehydration, ultraviolet
  • radiation, and physical damage.
  • Lower Cortex
  • Composed of tightly packed, dark-coloured fungal hypha.
  • Rhizines, which are fungal hyphae that extend downward to attach the lichen to its substrate.
  • Anchorage and Absorption. Its rhizines act as holdfasts, attaching the lichen to rocks or trees.
  • They also play a role in absorbing water and minerals. (Liberal valuation).

questions.question: Describe the thallus structure and vegetative reproduction of Saccharomyces
questions.solution_html:
• • Thallus Structure
  • All yeasts, including the species of Saccharomyces, are unicellular. The vegetative cells are
  • generally diploid. Even though the cells appear colorless individually, on artificial solid media
  • colonies appear as white, cream coloured or tinged with brownish pigment. The cells contain a large
  • membrane bound vacuole and a small nucleus. Other inclusions are mitochondria, storage granules
  • endoplasmic reticulum
  • • Vegetative Reproduction
  • In yeasts asexual reproduction is by budding.The cells of Saccharomyces can give rise to buds from
  • all over the surface. The point of origin of buds is at the poles of the yeast cell. Possibly it is because
  • the internal fluid pressure in an ellipsoidal cell is exerted maximally against the cell wall at the point
  • of maximum curvature. The cell wall then bulges and stretches out to form the bud.
questions.final_answer: of maximum curvature. The cell wall then bulges and stretches out to form the bud
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Describe in detail the vegetative body and asexual reproduction in Rhizopus.
questions.solution_html:
• The vegetative body in Rhizopus
  • ▪ The vegetative structure is mycelial; hyphae are branched and coenocytic.
  • ▪ The characteristic feature is the presence of rhizoids at the base of sporangiophores and the
  • stoloniferous habit of mycelium.
  • ▪ Aerial hyphae when touch the substratum bears rhizoids and sporangiophores.
  • ▪ The mycelium is differentiated into rhizoids, stolons and sporangiophores.
  • ▪ The rhizoids are repeatedly branched, penetrate the substratum and anchor the mycelium.
  • ▪ The stolons are aerial and arching, running horizontally and parallel to the substratum. At some
  • points of contact with the substrate, the stolons develop tufts of rhizoids and enter into the
  • substratum.
  • ▪ The sporangiophores grow upwards from the stolons exactly opposite the rhizoids, singly or in
  • clusters.
  • The asexual reproduction in Rhizopus
  • ▪ It occurs by means of aplanospores produced in the sporangia. The sporangiophores develop
  • opposite to the rhizoids
  • ▪ Sporangia develop terminally on sporangiophores which may be simple or branched.
  • ▪ The apex of aerial hypha swells and cytoplasmic mass along with nuclei move into this part.
  • ▪ The swollen part enlarges and develops into a large, globose structure, and it is the young
  • sporangium.
  • ▪ At the time of spore release, the sporangial wall cracks into a number of small fragments, the
  • columella collapses and the spores are quickly blown away by wind.
questions.final_answer: columella collapses and the spores are quickly blown away by wind
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Discuss the role of fungi in the production of alcohol, beer, wine, and fermented food products.
questions.solution_html:
• products.
  • Alcohol: Saccharomyces, the yeast ferments sugars (glucose, sucrose, maltose) into ethanol and
  • carbon dioxide under anaerobic conditions.
  • Beer: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (top-fermenting yeast) or Saccharomyces carlsbergensis (bottom
  • fermenting yeast)
  • ▪ Malting: Barley grains are germinated to produce enzymes that convert starch into maltose.
  • ▪ Mashing: The malt is mixed with water to form wort (a sugar-rich liquid).
  • ▪ Fermentation: Yeast ferments the sugars in the wort into ethanol and CO₂, producing beer
  • Wine
  • ▪ Natural or inoculated yeast ferments the sugars (mainly glucose and fructose) in grape juice to
  • ethanol and CO₂. The alcohol dissolves the metabolites forming the wine.
  • ▪ The type of yeast, sugar content, and fermentation conditions influence the flavour, aroma, and
  • alcohol content.
  • Secondary fermentation (in sparkling wines) adds carbonation
  • Fermented food products
  • ▪ Bread: Saccharomyces cerevisiae ferments sugars in dough, releasing CO₂ that causes the dough
  • to rise.
  • ▪ Cheese: Molds such as Penicillium roquefortii (blue cheese) and P.camemberti (Camembert)
  • develop characteristic flavours and textures.
  • ▪ Soy sauce and miso: Aspergillus oryzae breaks down starches and proteins during fermentation.
  • Rhizopus oligosporus ferments soybeans into a protein-rich, digestible product. (Liberal 4
  • valuation). e g

questions.question: Discuss the role of fungi in the production of alcohol, beer, wine, and fermented food products.
questions.solution_html:
• products.
  • Alcohol: Saccharomyces, the yeast ferments sugars (glucose, sucrose, maltose) into ethanol and
  • carbon dioxide under anaerobic conditions.
  • Beer: Saccharomyces cerevisiae (top-fermenting yeast) or Saccharomyces carlsbergensis (bottom
  • fermenting yeast)
  • ▪ Malting: Barley grains are germinated to produce enzymes that convert starch into maltose.
  • ▪ Mashing: The malt is mixed with water to form wort (a sugar-rich liquid).
  • ▪ Fermentation: Yeast ferments the sugars in the wort into ethanol and CO₂, producing beer
  • Wine
  • ▪ Natural or inoculated yeast ferments the sugars (mainly glucose and fructose) in grape juice to
  • ethanol and CO₂. The alcohol dissolves the metabolites forming the wine.
  • ▪ The type of yeast, sugar content, and fermentation conditions influence the flavour, aroma, and
  • alcohol content.
  • Secondary fermentation (in sparkling wines) adds carbonation
  • Fermented food products
  • ▪ Bread: Saccharomyces cerevisiae ferments sugars in dough, releasing CO₂ that causes the dough
  • to rise.
  • ▪ Cheese: Molds such as Penicillium roquefortii (blue cheese) and P.camemberti (Camembert)
  • develop characteristic flavours and textures.
  • ▪ Soy sauce and miso: Aspergillus oryzae breaks down starches and proteins during fermentation.
  • Rhizopus oligosporus ferments soybeans into a protein-rich, digestible product. (Liberal 4
